newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian traders wary on Cargill barter with North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders wary on Cargill barter with North Korea.

text.p: Asian traders familiar with doing business with North Korea said Tuesday they were sceptical about plans by American grain giant Cargill Inc. to barter as much as two million tons of grain with Pyongyang.
"According to our experience, trade with North Korea will face great difficulty, such as honouring agreements and making payments," said an official at a South Korean trading house.

Cargill, the world's largest private grain-trading company, said Monday that it was awaiting a decision by the U.S. Treasury on an application to barter grain for North Korean commodities. An initial 500,000-ton grain shipment was envisaged.

Minneapolis-based Cargill said the application, submitted in September, simply sought authorisation for barter dealing of some food product but did not specify whether rice, corn or other commodities would be traded.
U.S. officials have said they are considering easing trade sanctions against North Korea -- which is reeling from flood-induced food shortages -- to allow barter deals.
One Hong Kong-based grains trader said securing payment from North Korea for barter trade would not be easy.
"Banks in North Korea are not reliable and letters of credit can be worthless," he said.
"The logistics are terrible and the risk is enormous," he added, noting that the quality of goods received from North Korea in a barter exchange was difficult to control.
In one instance, a barter deal previously arranged by the trader fell through, resulting in losses.
"They got the cargo of wheat, we never got the cargo of metals and the guy just disappeared," he said.
